Meeting header:
Date: 2025-03-10 17:00 PT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Miguel Torres (Redwood SE), Sofia Chen (Product); Aisha Khan (CTO, Graystone), Ben Liu (ML Engineer), Ravi Patel (Infra Lead), Samira Das (PM)

Optional summary (auto-gen, may be rough):

Transcript:
[00:00:03] Lena: All right hi everyone, thanks for taking time, this is Lena from Redwood, i'm gonna kick off real quick, our SE Miguel is gonna run through some edge-case demos we promised — long context, high t p s loads and streaming backpressure stuff.
[00:00:20] Aisha: Hi Lena, thanks. To set context quickly, we have a product that ingests long multi-document medical reports, and we need persistent context across a session, sometimes 50–80k tokens. Also, burst traffic during morning reports, like 1.5–2k rps briefly, and p95 latency targets around 250ms for short queries.
[00:00:38] Miguel: Awesome thank you, that's exactly the kind of scenario we wanted to show. Quick confirmation: are you currently using hosted endpoints or self-hosted infra?
[00:00:46] Ben: We are on a mix — experiments on VM-based endpoints in cloud, but most traffic goes through our API gateways. We're evaluating a dedicated pool for production.
[00:00:54] Lena: Cool. We'll show both hosted and Dedicated options; also cover private VPC deployment notes for when you need to keep data in your network.
[00:01:05] Miguel: Opening the demo deck — please forgive some screen lag, it's a live demo. First slide, long context strategy: we do prefix streaming, KV cache snapshots, and dynamic windowing so you don't have to keep sending 80k tokens every request. For example, we can keep the last N chunks in the KV cache on the GPU and serve continued generation with O(1) token access.
[00:01:30] Samira: When you say KV cache snapshots, is that persisted across restarts or only in-memory GPU cache?
[00:01:36] Miguel: Good question. Primary cache is in GPU memory for performance; we also have optional checkpointing to object store so warm starts are fast. In Dedicated you can pin the checkpoint strategy, in hosted we manage checkpointing with configurable retention.
[00:01:50] Ravi: How do you handle eviction if we have thousands of sessions all with long contexts — won't memory blow up?
[00:01:56] Miguel: We use a tiered policy — hot KV on GPU for active sessions, warm on local SSDs for recently active, and cold in object store. We also expose eviction knobs and LRU TTLs. For extreme scale you can set session affinity to spread across a pool, or move to shard-by-customer.
[00:02:12] [00:02:12] Ben: okay that helps. latency wise any numbers?
[00:02:17] Miguel: For continuations with KV hit and modest prompt size p50 is single-digit ms for token emission, p95 depends on model and seq len. We have internal benchmarks — happy to share the spreadsheet — but practical numbers: for a 32k context model with KV hit we see p95 token latency of ~30–70ms on A100-equivalent Dedicated nodes under moderate load. Under heavy multi-tenant hosted load it can be higher.
[00:02:40] Aisha: Understood — another concern is streaming backpressure. Our front end streams tokens to users and we sometimes see backpressure when network clients are slow — how do you manage client-side slow consumers?
[00:02:52] Miguel: Right, streaming backpressure is tricky. Our runtime supports backpressure-aware streaming where we chunk outputs and enforce a bounded send queue. If a client is slow we can pause generation or buffer up to a configurable threshold and apply backpressure to upstream requests. For critical low-latency paths we recommend per-route timeout + partial-output guarantees — so you either get first N tokens quickly or a graceful cutoff with continuation token to resume later.
[00:03:17] Ben: So you pause generation server-side when network stalls? Does that tie up GPU resources?
[00:03:22] Miguel: If you pause, yes the GPU session holds the KV state; to avoid resource hogging we offer two patterns: 1) short pauses with session keepalive timers, 2) snapshot-and-evict where we checkpoint and release GPU (with a cold-start cost to resume). Those are knobs you can tune based on your SLOs.
[00:03:39] [00:03:39] Ravi: For our use case we cannot have many warm sessions due to cost, so snapshot-and-evict seems preferable. Any typical resume times?
[00:03:46] Miguel: Resume depends on snapshot retrieval and warming — in Dedicated with local SSD it's ~200–800ms, in hosted cold path with object store could be 1.2–2.5s. We'll share concrete numbers from our benchmark doc.
[00:03:59] Samira: Timeouts — sometimes our orchestration has 30s request timeouts. How do you handle long-running generations?
[00:04:06] Miguel: You should use streaming + resumable generation. Redwood supports chunked responses and a continuation token model: if a request times out, client can call a resume endpoint with token to pick up. Also we support background jobs for really long tasks with callback/webhook on completion.
[00:04:18] [00:04:18] Aisha: Okay demo time please
[00:04:21] Miguel: Switching to the console — note the UI has per-route timeout, max tokens, and backpressure settings. I'll run a live load demo: first, long-context session. I'm uploading a 60k-token bundle (note: generator sim, not real PHI).
[00:04:40] [00:04:40] System noise / screen share lag
[00:04:45] Miguel: Starting generation with KV warm. You can see streaming chunks arrive in the console panel with timestamps. We'll intentionally throttle the simulated client to force backpressure — watch queue size and the 'pause' event in the trace.
[00:05:05] Ben: yep i see pause, and then resume after a second. There's a note 'evicted to cold store' — what's that?
[00:05:12] Miguel: That's the snapshot-and-evict path. It reduced GPU usage, then a resume pulled the snapshot back.
[00:05:18] [00:05:18] Aisha: Any cost delta between keeping session hot vs snapshot-evict?
[00:05:22] Miguel: Hot sessions cost more due to pinned GPU memory and slot concurrency. Snapshot-evict trades small storage+resume latency for lower steady cost. We can run a cost model for your observed session durations.
[00:05:33] Miguel: Now switching to high TPS demo. We'll run a synthetic load of 2k rps with short prompts to emulate morning burst. Note this is on a dedicated pool we've provisioned for the demo; behavior on hosted will be similar but multi-tenant noise can add variability.
[00:05:50] [00:05:50] Miguel: Launching load generator...
[00:05:57] [00:05:57] System: micro-bursts start
[00:06:05] Miguel: You can see autoscaler kicking — in Dedicated we allow predictor-based autoscaling + buffer capacity for bursts. For strict p95 SLOs you'd choose reserved throughput capacity.
[00:06:17] Ben: What's the difference between buffer capacity and reserved? If we want deterministic p95, do we need reserved commit?
[00:06:23] Miguel: Buffer capacity is opportunistic spare GPUs we can attach; reserved commit is guaranteed capacity you pay for. For hard SLOs we recommend reserved Dedicated pools sized for your 99th percentile, with autoscale for rare extra bursts.
[00:06:34] Aisha: And how about batching? Can batching degrade p95? We need to keep sub-250ms for short prompts.
[00:06:41] Miguel: Batching increases throughput and lowers unit cost but adds a batching window latency. In our Optimize toolkit we suggest hybrid configs: small max batch sizes and dynamic batching based on real-time queue depth. For 250ms p95 you'd set max batch window to ~10–30ms and smaller batch sizes, sacrificing some cost efficiency.
[00:06:59] [00:06:59] Ben: Under heavy load did you observe queue-dropping or requests timing out?
[00:07:05] Miguel: We implement backpressure to upstream so we throttle early rather than drop silently — optional rejections with 429 and Retry-After headers. For critical routes you can set queuing policies — FIFO vs priority — and overflow destinations (e.g., write to background job queue).
[00:07:18] Ravi: For compliance we need audit logs and tenant isolation, plus keys in our HSM. Does Redwood support customer KMS/HSM?
[00:07:26] Miguel: Yes — for Private and Dedicated we integrate with customer KMS/HSM for key wrapping; we also emit detailed audit logs and can send them to your SIEM. For hosted we offer bring-your-own key patterns and redaction options.
[00:07:40] Samira: What about SOC2/ISO?
[00:07:43] Lena: We're SOC 2 Type II and pursuing ISO; i'll attach the compliance pack after the call.
[00:07:48] [00:07:48] Aisha: On networking, do we get direct VPC peering or private link?
[00:07:53] Miguel: We offer VPC peering, PrivateLink equivalents, and an on-prem package for air-gapped environments. Private deployments can run behind your firewall.
[00:08:03] Ben: Quick question — model variants: you mentioned fallback to quantized models during overloads. Will that change semantics significantly?
[00:08:12] Miguel: We provide model variant profiles and quality delta estimates. For many workloads 4-bit quantized variants are near-identical for generation distribution; for sensitive outputs you can pin a full-precision model or run A/B quality checks via Optimize. We also have automatic fallback policies: e.g. prefer fp16 then int4 with a per-customer tolerance threshold.
[00:08:29] [00:08:29] Aisha: Can you show logs for a case where fallback happened?
[00:08:33] Miguel: Yep pulling a recent incident — here you see route-level trace: increased latency triggered fallback to quantized variant, downstream quality guard raised an alert and we rolled back after traffic subsided.
[00:08:46] Ben: Nice. are there SDKs for resumable tokens?
[00:08:49] Miguel: Yes we have js/python SDK helpers for resume tokens, and example code in our docs. I'll paste the link in chat.
[00:08:58] [00:08:58] Chat: https://redwood.ai/docs/resumable-generation
[00:09:05] Aisha: Alright big-picture: we like dedicated pool but want a clear way to run benchmarks against our payloads before commit. Can Redwood run a week-long benchmark?
[00:09:14] Lena: Absolutely; our SE bench program provisions a sandbox dedicated pool and runs your real payloads. Miguel, we offered that last time for another enterprise — what's the checklist?
[00:09:22] Miguel: We'll need payload patterns (size distribution, seq len), concurrency curves, SLO targets (p95/p99), and security constraints. We'll then run a 3–7 day soak with headroom and produce cost/latency/regression reports.
[00:09:35] Samira: timeline for that — we want to pilot in next sprint (~2 weeks).
[00:09:40] Lena: If we get data this week we can spin up bench within 7–10 days, so pilot aligns.
[00:09:46] [00:09:46] Ben: any gotchas for our infra team?
[00:09:49] Ravi: our infra uses strict egress rules, will that break hosted?
[00:09:53] Miguel: For hosted you'd need minimal egress to Redwood endpoints; for stricter networks use Private deployment in your VPC. We can run a checklist with ports, certs, and peering steps.
[00:10:05] [00:10:05] 10-minute mark — demo continues with deeper logs and traces (omitted some repeated screen steps)
[00:10:35] Miguel: A quick note on throttling: we expose per-customer quotas and token-rate throttles; combined with queuing policies you can avoid overload cascades.
[00:10:45] Ben: For p95 250ms, will tokenization cost add variance? We have NFKC normalization and often send pre-tokenized payloads.
[00:10:55] Miguel: If you pre-tokenize you save a few ms; our runtimes accept pre-tokenized frames via the API. That helps with predictability.
[00:11:03] [00:11:03] Aisha: Security question: are transcripts retained, and can we opt-out or set retention?
[00:11:08] Lena: Yes, retention is configurable; hosted defaults to 30 days for telemetry, but Enterprise plans can set custom retention and full deletion on request. We'll include retention policy in the pack.
[00:11:19] Miguel: Closing the demo — quick recap of edge-case guidance: 1) use KV + snapshot for long context 2) tune batching and buffer for TPS vs cost balance 3) use resumable streaming to handle timeouts 4) reserve capacity for strict SLOs and use priority queuing/backpressure to avoid silent drops.
[00:11:43] [00:11:43] Aisha: sounds good. A couple small follow-ups: can the bench include a cold-start/resume SLA matrix?
[00:11:49] Miguel: Yes we'll measure cold->warm resume times across storage tiers and include it in the report.
[00:11:55] Lena: All right let's do next steps and responsibilities — I'll summarize.
[00:11:59] [00:11:59] Recap / Next steps (verbatim):
- Lena: Send pricing and security docs (SOC2 pack + ISO notes) by 2025-03-12
- Miguel: Draft benchmark plan and checklist; propose Dedicated pool sizing by 2025-03-14
- Graystone (Ben/Ravi): Share payload histograms, concurrency curves, and SLO targets by 2025-03-12
- Schedule: bench to start pending data, target pilot in ~2 weeks

[00:12:25] Aisha: Thanks everyone, appreciate the practicality.
[00:12:28] Lena: Thanks all — i'll drop links and the pricing doc after the call.
[00:12:33] [00:12:33] Meeting ends
